title: Integral local system and its scalar extensions
notes: Over a nonsingular complex analytic space \(S\), the notes take a locally free finite-rank sheaf \(H_{\mathbb Z}\), form \(H_{\mathbb C}=H_{\mathbb Z}\otimes\mathbb C\), \(H_{\mathbb R}\), and \(H_{\mathcal O}=H_{\mathbb Z}\otimes\mathcal O_S\), and call a local system a bundle with connection.
statement: An integral local system is a sheaf locally isomorphic to \(\underline{\mathbb Z}^{,r}\). Tensoring over \(\mathbb Z\) with the constant real or complex sheaf gives local systems; \(\mathcal H=H_{\mathbb Z}\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathcal O_S\) is a holomorphic vector bundle. Locally constant complex sheaves correspond to holomorphic bundles with integrable holomorphic connection; an integral structure is additional data.
reconstruction: The word integrable (equivalently flat) is necessary in the connection equivalence. The complex local system and its associated holomorphic bundle must be distinguished, although the notebook sometimes writes \(H_{\mathbb C}\) for both.
fate: The exposition predates this talk: \citet[\S2, pp.~232--235]{griffiths1970periods} summarizes the period-domain formalism in an invited lecture delivered on 29 August 1968, received on 18 September 1969, and published in March 1970.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: standard local-system/VHS terminology; no research problem is posed.

title: Canonical flat connection and horizontal sections
notes: The displayed connection is \(\nabla:H_{\mathcal O}\to\Omega_S^1\otimes_{\mathcal O_S}H_{\mathcal O}\), called Gauss--Manin; the kernel is the sheaf of locally constant complex sections.
statement: For a complex local system \(L\), the associated bundle \(\mathcal H=L\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathcal O_S\) has the flat connection \(\nabla(v\otimes f)=v\otimes df\), with \(\ker\nabla=L\). For a smooth proper family, the construction applied to a cohomology local system is the Gauss--Manin connection.
reconstruction: The first construction needs no family. The name Gauss--Manin is geometrically justified only after identifying the local system with the cohomology of such a family; the notes do not supply a family here. This repeats the setting of 1969-182.2 and 1971-251.5.
fate: The exposition predates this talk: \citet[\S2, pp.~232--235]{griffiths1970periods} summarizes the period-domain formalism in an invited lecture delivered on 29 August 1968, received on 18 September 1969, and published in March 1970. Its formula (2.1) records the connection's compatibility with the Hodge filtration.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: the local-system construction and its geometric Gauss--Manin specialization remain standard.

title: Hodge filtration and Griffiths transversality
notes: A decreasing filtration \(F^0\supset F^1\supset\cdots\supset F^n\) by holomorphic subbundles is required to satisfy \(\nabla\mathcal F^p\subset\Omega_S^1\otimes\mathcal F^{p-1}\). A locally constant bilinear form is to give a polarized Hodge structure in each fibre.
statement: A polarized integral variation of pure Hodge structure of weight \(n\) consists of an integral local system, holomorphic subbundles \(F^p\mathcal H\), a flat bilinear form \(Q\), fibrewise Hodge opposition and positivity, and \(\nabla(F^p\mathcal H)\subset\Omega_S^1\otimes F^{p-1}\mathcal H\). The displayed finite range presupposes effective Hodge types \(0\leq p,q\leq n\); the general definition uses all integer indices, with eventually constant endpoints.
reconstruction: The bundle \(\mathcal H\), not a locally constant sheaf, carries the holomorphic filtration. Flatness and the effective-weight convention make explicit the notebook's abbreviated notation.
fate: The exposition predates this talk: \citet[\S2, pp.~232--235]{griffiths1970periods} summarizes the period-domain formalism in an invited lecture delivered on 29 August 1968, received on 18 September 1969, and published in March 1970. See equation (2.1) for transversality and the preceding definition of the classifying space.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established definition; the notes do not pose a transversality conjecture.

title: Compact dual and the erroneous orthogonality index
notes: The notes impose fixed flag dimensions and the displayed condition \(\psi(F^p,F^{n-p})=0\). The original P000451 scan has this same index, without \(+1\).
statement: Fix a real vector space \(H_{\mathbb R}\), Hodge numbers of weight \(n\), and a nondegenerate \((-1)^n\)-symmetric bilinear form \(Q\). The compact dual is the projective variety of flags with the prescribed dimensions and \(Q(F^p,F^{n-p+1})=0\) for every \(p\), taking the appropriate connected flag component if needed.

The bilinear relations and flag-domain construction in \S2 support the corrected formulation, not the literal index.

title: Opposed filtrations, Hodge decomposition, and Weil operator
notes: The page imposes \(F^p\oplus\overline{F^{n-p+1}}=H_{\mathbb C}\), defines \(H^{p,n-p}=F^p\cap\overline{F^{n-p}}\), and lets \(C\) act by \(i^{2p-n}\) on this summand.

reconstruction: The direct-sum decomposition and recovery of the filtration are stated explicitly to unpack the notebook's concise definition; the notation and exponent themselves are faithful.

title: Polarization positivity and the open period domain
notes: The form \(\psi(x,C\bar x)\) is positive, and imposing this positivity and opposition gives an open subset \(D\) of the compact flag variety \(\overline D\).
statement: Normalize the real polarization \(Q\) so that \(h(x,y)=Q(x,C\overline y)\) is a positive-definite Hermitian form. For fixed polarized Hodge numbers and fixed \(Q\), the flags satisfying Hodge opposition and this positivity form an open complex submanifold \(D\) of the compact dual. Its connected components may be selected separately.
reconstruction: The harmless overall sign convention for \(Q\) is fixed explicitly; positivity means for every nonzero complex vector. Integrality of a lattice does not make the period domain discrete.
fate: The exposition predates this talk: \citet[\S2, pp.~232--235]{griffiths1970periods} summarizes the period-domain formalism in an invited lecture delivered on 29 August 1968, received on 18 September 1969, and published in March 1970.

title: Homogeneous period domain and compact stabilizer
notes: The real group preserving \(\psi\) acts transitively on \(D\); the stabilizer \(H\) is compact.
statement: Let \(G_{\mathbb R}\) be the full real isometry group of the polarization with the relevant flag-component action. A period-domain orbit is \(G_{\mathbb R}/V\), where the stabilizer \(V\) of a polarized Hodge decomposition is compact. The identity component \(G_{\mathbb R}^{0}\) acts transitively on each connected component of the period domain.
reconstruction: The notebook's stabilizer \(H\) is renamed \(V\) to distinguish it from the Hodge vector space. Connected-component qualifications are necessary if one replaces the full real isometry group by its identity component; the continuation on P000458 does so.

title: Projection to a Riemannian symmetric space
notes: For a maximal compact \(K\supset H\), the map \(G/H\to G/K\) is said not to be holomorphic; the following sentence says \(G/K\) has a complex structure.
statement: A maximal compact subgroup \(K\) containing the compact period stabilizer \(V\) gives a smooth fibration \(K/V\to G_{\mathbb R}/V\to G_{\mathbb R}/K\). The base is a Riemannian symmetric space and is not, in general, Hermitian symmetric. In the Hermitian cases the projection need not be holomorphic; when \(V=K\), it is the identity and is holomorphic for the compatible structure.
reconstruction: Both universal assertions need qualification. No complex structure on the symmetric space is supplied in the notes. The correct general statement is smooth homogeneity, with additional hypotheses for complex geometry.
fate: The exposition predates this talk: \citet[\S2, pp.~232--235]{griffiths1970periods} summarizes the period-domain formalism in an invited lecture delivered on 29 August 1968, received on 18 September 1969, and published in March 1970. Equation (2.3) explicitly describes a differentiable fibration and qualifies holomorphicity; it does not assert that every symmetric quotient is complex.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: the literal blanket claim is false; the qualified period-domain fibration is classical.

title: Local field, valuation ring, and projective linear action
notes: The uncancelled text takes \(K\) to be a finite extension of \(\mathbb Q_p\), with integer ring \(A\), maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m\), and fractional linear transformations of \(\mathbb P^1(K)\).
statement: For a finite extension \(K/\mathbb Q_p\), put \(A=\mathcal O_K\), \(\mathfrak m=(\pi)\), and \(k=A/\mathfrak m\cong\mathbb F_q\). Then \(G=\mathrm{PGL}_2(K)=\mathrm{GL}_2(K)/K^\times\) acts on \(\mathbb P^1(K)\) by \(z\mapsto(az+b)/(cz+d)\), with the usual interpretation at poles and infinity.
reconstruction: Invertibility of the representing matrix and the projective convention at infinity are made explicit. The construction also works for equal-characteristic local fields, but that extension is editorial: the relevant phrase is cancelled in the original.
fate: The local-field tree was already part of the established theory: \citet[Introduction, pp.~130--131, and \S1]{mumford1972degenerating} uses the lattice tree and its \(q+1\) neighbours in a paper received on 16 March 1971 and published in 1972. \citet[Chapter~II]{serre1977arbres} is a later systematic exposition based on his 1968--1969 Coll\`ege de France course; its 1977 publication is not the construction's first circulation.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: standard local-field setting and projective action; no open question.

title: Lattices, homothety classes, and the vertex homogeneous space
notes: A lattice is written \(L=Ae_1\oplus Ae_2\); lattices are equivalent when they differ by a scalar in \(K^\times\). Vertices are these equivalence classes, also written \(G/U\) for \(U=\mathrm{GL}_2(A)/A^\times\).
statement: A full lattice in \(K^2\) is a finitely generated \(A\)-submodule spanning \(K^2\), necessarily free of rank two. The homothety classes form a transitive \(G\)-set. The stabilizer of \([A^2]\) is the image of \(K^\times\mathrm{GL}_2(A)\) in \(G\), naturally \(\mathrm{GL}_2(A)/A^\times\); hence the vertex set is \(G/U\).
reconstruction: Fullness and spanning are essential: a rank-two module embedded degenerately would not define the intended vertex. The stabilizer identification unpacks the concise quotient notation.

title: Adjacency and the q plus one neighbours
notes: Two vertices are joined when their distance is one, and exactly \(q+1\) edges meet at each vertex.
statement: The neighbours of \([L]\) are represented uniquely by sublattices \(L'\) with \(\pi L\subsetneq L'\subsetneq L\). They correspond to one-dimensional subspaces of \(L/\pi L\cong k^2\), so there are \(|\mathbb P^1(k)|=q+1\) neighbours.

title: The lattice graph is a tree
notes: The graph \(\Delta\) is called a connected graph without cycles, with its natural \(G\)-action.
statement: The graph of homothety classes of full rank-two \(A\)-lattices and distance-one edges is connected and acyclic. Its graph metric is the elementary-divisor metric, and the action of \(\mathrm{PGL}_2(K)\) preserves adjacency. Thus its geometric realization is the Bruhat--Tits tree in rank one.

notes: The heading cites \ru{ст. Тэйта, Математика, 13:2, \S3} and defines \(\mathbb C_p\) as the completion of an algebraic closure of \(\mathbb Q_p\).

title: Finite local Galois extensions and normalized valuation
notes: The notes write \(K/\mathbb Q_p\) and \(L/K\) finite, set \(G=\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)\), introduce their integer and residue rings, and choose \(|\pi|=|k|^{-1}\).
statement: Let \(K/\mathbb Q_p\) be finite and let \(L/K\) be finite Galois. Write \(\mathcal O_K,\mathcal O_L\) for integer rings, \(\mathfrak m_K=(\pi),\mathfrak m_L=(\tau)\), and \(k,\ell\) for residue fields. Normalize \(|\pi|_K=|k|^{-1}\), and use its unique extension to \(L\); every element of \(G\) preserves this valuation and \(\mathcal O_L\).
reconstruction: The Galois hypothesis is supplied because it is needed for the surjectivity onto \(\operatorname{Gal}(\ell/k)\) asserted later. Simply naming the automorphism group of an arbitrary finite extension is not enough. The valuation on \(L\) here extends the chosen one on \(K\), rather than being independently normalized by \(|\ell|\).
fate: This is classical local ramification theory, already organized in Serre's 1962 \emph{Corps locaux}; the opened English edition is \citet[Chapter~IV, pp.~61--79]{serre1979local}. The precise formulas and proofs were read in \citet[Lemma~7.57, Theorem~7.58, and Corollary~7.59, pp.~130--131]{milne2020ant}; this modern check is not evidence of a later discovery.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: standard local-field setup with the Galois hypothesis made explicit.

title: Ramification filtration and its shifted indexing
notes: The definition is \(G_i=\{g:\ g(x)-x\in\mathfrak m_L^i\text{ for every }x\in\mathcal O_L\}\), with \(G=G_0\supset G_1\supset\cdots\supset\{1\}\); every \(G_i\) is normal.
statement: For the finite Galois extension just specified, define \(G_i^{\rm note}\) by that formula for \(i\geq0\). These are normal subgroups of \(G\), eventually trivial. They satisfy \(G_0^{\rm note}=G\) and \(G_i^{\rm note}=G_{i-1}^{\rm lower}\) for \(i\geq1\), where the conventional lower filtration has inertia at index zero.
reconstruction: The shifted indexing is intentional and consistent across both pages; it is not silently changed. Eventual triviality follows from finiteness of \(G\) and separation of the valuation topology, not from a fixed universal length.
fate: This is classical local ramification theory, already organized in Serre's 1962 \emph{Corps locaux}; the opened English edition is \citet[Chapter~IV, pp.~61--79]{serre1979local}. title: Residue-field quotient and the exercise on surjectivity
notes: Reduction gives \(\psi:G\to\operatorname{Gal}(\ell/k)\); its kernel is \(G_1\), and proving that the induced injection \(G_0/G_1\to\operatorname{Gal}(\ell/k)\) is an isomorphism is left as an exercise.

The quotient is cyclic, generated by the finite-field Frobenius. A residue element must be lifted to \(\mathcal O_L\); kernel membership means fixing every residue element.

The exercise is a classical expository task with a definite known answer, not a new research problem; it is therefore indexed as an occurrence but not assigned a new problem identifier.

title: Tame character on the first inertia quotient
notes: The map \(g\mapsto\overline{g(\tau)/\tau}\) is said to identify \(G_1/G_2\) with a subgroup of \(\ell^\times\), independently of the uniformizer.
statement: For \(g\in G_1^{\rm note}\), let \(\chi(g)=\overline{g(\tau)/\tau}\in\ell^\times\). This is a homomorphism, its kernel is \(G_2^{\rm note}\), and it is independent of the uniformizer \(\tau\). Thus tame inertia \(G_1^{\rm note}/G_2^{\rm note}\) is cyclic of order prime to the residue characteristic.

fate: This is classical local ramification theory, already organized in Serre's 1962 \emph{Corps locaux}; the opened English edition is \citet[Chapter~IV, pp.~61--79]{serre1979local}. The precise formulas and proofs were read in \citet[Lemma~7.57, Theorem~7.58, and Corollary~7.59, pp.~130--131]{milne2020ant}; this modern check is not evidence of a later discovery. See Milne's Corollary~7.59 and its first character computation.

title: Additive characters on higher ramification quotients
notes: For \(i\geq2\), the notes use \(\overline{(g(\tau)/\tau-1)/\tau^{i-1}}\in\ell\) and state that its kernel is \(G_{i+1}\), although the displayed domain is already \(G_i/G_{i+1}\).
statement: For \(i\geq2\), the map \(c_i:G_i^{\rm note}\to(\ell,+)\), \(c_i(g)=\overline{(g(\tau)-\tau)/\tau^i}\), is a homomorphism with kernel \(G_{i+1}^{\rm note}\). Consequently \(G_i^{\rm note}/G_{i+1}^{\rm note}\) embeds in the additive residue group and is an elementary abelian \(p\)-group.
reconstruction: The character's domain is repaired before taking the quotient; an injective map defined on \(G_i/G_{i+1}\) has trivial kernel, not \(G_{i+1}\). Unlike the tame character, these coordinate-valued higher characters can change with the uniformizer, although the quotient statement is intrinsic.
fate: This is classical local ramification theory, already organized in Serre's 1962 \emph{Corps locaux}; the opened English edition is \citet[Chapter~IV, pp.~61--79]{serre1979local}. The precise formulas and proofs were read in \citet[Lemma~7.57, Theorem~7.58, and Corollary~7.59, pp.~130--131]{milne2020ant}; this modern check is not evidence of a later discovery. The same calculation, with the usual one-place shift, is the second part of Milne's Corollary~7.59.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: the higher quotient theorem is standard; the literal domain/kernel combination is inconsistent.

title: Solvability of finite local Galois groups
notes: Kazhdan announces that the filtration will show \(G\) is solvable; every successive quotient is declared abelian.
statement: For every finite Galois extension \(L/K\) of nonarchimedean local fields with finite residue field, \(\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)\) is solvable: the residue quotient is cyclic, the tame quotient is cyclic, and the remaining finite filtration has elementary abelian \(p\)-quotients.
reconstruction: The finite residue field and Galois assumptions are essential to this precise formulation; the statement is not a theorem about arbitrary discretely valued fields or arbitrary global number fields.
fate: This is classical local ramification theory, already organized in Serre's 1962 \emph{Corps locaux}; the opened English edition is \citet[Chapter~IV, pp.~61--79]{serre1979local}. title: Constant sheaf and its étalé space
notes: The constant sheaf \(\mathbb Z\) has constant-number sections over a connected domain; it is associated to the presheaf \(U\mapsto\mathbb Z\). Its sheaf space is written \(S\times\mathbb Z\).
statement: On a complex manifold \(S\), the constant sheaf \(\underline{\mathbb Z}\) is the sheaf of locally constant integer-valued functions, equivalently the sheafification of the constant presheaf. Its \(\acute{e}\)tal\'{e} space is \(S\times\mathbb Z\), with \(\mathbb Z\) discrete. On a connected nonempty open set its sections are \(\mathbb Z\); on a disconnected open set they need not be globally constant.
reconstruction: The sheafification and connected-open qualification are part of the mathematical distinction being explained in the notes, not a new theorem. The empty set convention for the constant presheaf is immaterial after sheafification.
fate: The exposition predates this talk: \citet[\S2, pp.~232--235]{griffiths1970periods} summarizes the period-domain formalism in an invited lecture delivered on 29 August 1968, received on 18 September 1969, and published in March 1970. This elementary local-system background underlies the bundle formulation used there.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: standard sheaf theory and the intended foundation for the Hodge discussion.

title: Integral local systems from locally constant transition functions
notes: Locally \(H_{\mathbb Z}|_U\cong U\times\mathbb Z^n\), \(\Gamma(U,H_{\mathbb Z})\cong\mathbb Z^n\), and transition functions take values in \(\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb Z)\); connectedness of \(S\) makes the rank constant.
statement: A rank-\(r\) integral local system is obtained by gluing constant sheaves on a trivializing cover with locally constant \(\mathrm{GL}_r(\mathbb Z)\)-valued transition functions satisfying the cocycle condition. Its rank is locally constant, hence constant on connected \(S\). The section formula \(\Gamma(U,H_{\mathbb Z})\cong\mathbb Z^r\) holds for connected trivializing \(U\).
reconstruction: The displayed product is the local \(\acute{e}\)tal\'{e}-space model; \(U\) must be connected for the asserted section group. The cocycle condition is implicit in the gluing language and is stated explicitly here.
fate: The exposition predates this talk: \citet[\S2, pp.~232--235]{griffiths1970periods} summarizes the period-domain formalism in an invited lecture delivered on 29 August 1968, received on 18 September 1969, and published in March 1970. This revisits 1972-272.1 with a transition-function description.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: standard gluing description, not a newly posed classification problem.

title: Associated real, complex, and holomorphic bundles
notes: Using the same transition matrices, the notes construct \(H_{\mathbb R}\), \(H_{\mathbb C}\), and the sheaf \(H_{\mathcal O}\) of holomorphic sections, with \(H_{\mathcal O}=H_{\mathbb Z}\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathcal O_S\).
statement: Extend the transition matrices of an integral local system along \(\mathbb Z\subset\mathbb R\subset\mathbb C\). This produces real and complex flat vector bundles; the latter's locally constant transition functions are holomorphic and define a holomorphic bundle whose sheaf of sections is \(\mathcal H=H_{\mathbb Z}\otimes\mathcal O_S\).
reconstruction: The local system of flat sections, the total vector bundle, and the sheaf of all holomorphic sections are distinguished explicitly; the notebook uses one symbol in more than one of these senses.
fate: The exposition predates this talk: \citet[\S2, pp.~232--235]{griffiths1970periods} summarizes the period-domain formalism in an invited lecture delivered on 29 August 1968, received on 18 September 1969, and published in March 1970.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: the standard passage from integral monodromy to a flat holomorphic bundle.

title: Flat connection in a locally constant frame
notes:
The connection is \(\mathbb C\)-linear, satisfies \(
abla(\varphi f)=\varphi
abla f+d\varphi\otimes f\), and in a constant frame \(u_i\) is \(
abla\sum_i\varphi_i u_i=\sum_i d\varphi_i\otimes u_i\). Its curvature is zero.
statement: For a holomorphic bundle defined by locally constant transition matrices, the local operator \(d\) in each constant frame glues to a globally defined holomorphic connection. It is complex-linear, satisfies the displayed Leibniz rule, and its extension to bundle-valued forms has \(\nabla^2=0\). Its horizontal sheaf is exactly the initial complex local system.
reconstruction: The connection is not \(\mathcal O_S\)-linear; complex-linearity and the Leibniz rule are the correct axioms. Zero curvature is both explicitly stated and justified by the local formula, so it is not merely an omitted hypothesis here.
fate: The exposition predates this talk: \citet[\S2, pp.~232--235]{griffiths1970periods} summarizes the period-domain formalism in an invited lecture delivered on 29 August 1968, received on 18 September 1969, and published in March 1970. This expands the flat/Gauss--Manin construction in 1972-272.2.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: a complete standard local construction with no unresolved step.

title: Horizontal polarization and transversality of the Hodge filtration
notes: The holomorphic filtration is again required to satisfy Griffiths' condition, and a locally constant bilinear form \(\psi\) is required to produce a Hodge structure at every point.
statement: For the flat holomorphic bundle \((\mathcal H,\nabla)\), require decreasing holomorphic subbundles \(F^p\mathcal H\) with \(\nabla F^p\subset\Omega_S^1\otimes F^{p-1}\), and a flat bilinear form \(Q\). Together with fibrewise opposition, weight parity, and positivity, these give a polarized variation of pure Hodge structure.
reconstruction: The form's local constancy means \(\nabla Q=0\), and the filtration need not be flat. The later fibrewise relations, including the parity correction in the next item, are incorporated only as explicitly identified components of the definition.
fate: The exposition predates this talk: \citet[\S2, pp.~232--235]{griffiths1970periods} summarizes the period-domain formalism in an invited lecture delivered on 29 August 1968, received on 18 September 1969, and published in March 1970. The transversality equation is (2.1). This is a repeat of 1972-272.3, not an independent research problem.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: standard polarized variation; the notes' repetition is preserved in the occurrence index.

title: Parity of the polarization is reversed in the notebook
notes: The form is said to be symmetric for odd \(n\) and skew-symmetric for even \(n\). Both Russian and English transcriptions follow the handwriting.
statement: For a pure polarized Hodge structure of weight \(n\), the bilinear polarization satisfies \(Q(y,x)=(-1)^n Q(x,y)\): it is symmetric for even \(n\) and alternating for odd \(n\). With the notebook's Weil-operator convention, an overall real sign can be chosen so that \(Q(x,C\bar y)\) is positive Hermitian.
reconstruction: The parity reversal is a faithful mathematical error, not a translation correction. Changing an overall sign of \(Q\) cannot change symmetric into alternating; it therefore cannot explain the reversed statement.
fate: \citet[\S1, equations (1.7)--(1.15)]{griffiths1968periods1} gives the correct parity and bilinear relations before the talk; \citet[\S2]{griffiths1970periods} summarizes the same framework.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: the literal parity claim is false, and the standard correction is unambiguous.

title: Projective flag variety and the corrected isotropic compact dual
notes: For dimensions \(k_0\geq k_1\geq\cdots\geq k_n\), the flag space is projective algebraic. The following page now writes \(\psi(F^p,F^{n-p+1})=0\) with the correct index.
statement: In a fixed complex vector space, flags of dimensions \(k_p\) form a projective partial flag variety. Imposing the closed bilinear relations \(Q(F^p,F^{n-p+1})=0\), with dimensions compatible with a polarized weight-\(n\) Hodge structure, gives the compact dual; a connected component is chosen when necessary.
reconstruction: The dimensions are constrained by the intended Hodge numbers and the nondegenerate form; arbitrary numerical flags need not admit polarized Hodge points. P000458 corrects the earlier index internally, but does not explicitly announce an erratum.
fate: The exposition predates this talk: \citet[\S2, pp.~232--235]{griffiths1970periods} summarizes the period-domain formalism in an invited lecture delivered on 29 August 1968, received on 18 September 1969, and published in March 1970. The flag variety and the bilinear subvariety are separated here to make the algebraic and positivity conditions transparent.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: standard projective compact dual; the correct formula links back to the emendation of 1972-272.4.

title: Opposition, Weil operator, and positivity define the period domain
notes: The page imposes \(F^p\oplus\overline{F^{n-p+1}}=H_{\mathbb C}\), defines the Weil operator by Hodge type, requires \(\psi(x,C\bar y)\) positive Hermitian, and calls \(D\) open in \(\overline D\).
statement: After correcting the parity of \(Q\), the opposition identities recover the Hodge decomposition; let \(C|_{H^{p,n-p}}=i^{2p-n}\). The flags for which \(Q(x,C\bar y)\) is positive definite form the period domain, open in the isotropic compact dual, determined by the Hodge numbers and the fixed real polarization form.
reconstruction: This combines the page's related fibrewise defining relations into one item, while retaining parity and the compact-dual construction as separate claims because each has its own correction or hypothesis.
fate: The exposition predates this talk: \citet[\S2, pp.~232--235]{griffiths1970periods} summarizes the period-domain formalism in an invited lecture delivered on 29 August 1968, received on 18 September 1969, and published in March 1970.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: classical period-domain construction; this repeats 1972-272.5--6 with no new question.

title: Announced homogeneity and the identity-component qualification
notes: For next time, the complex isometry group is to be shown transitive on \(\overline D\), and the identity component of the real group transitive on \(D\).
statement: The relevant complex isometry group acts transitively on each appropriate isotropic flag orbit. The identity component \(G_{\mathbb R}^0\) acts transitively on a chosen connected component of the polarized period domain. If \(D\) denotes all components at once, transitivity of the identity component need not hold.
reconstruction: A connected-component choice is supplied. The notes announce an elementary homogeneous-space proof for a subsequent meeting; they do not formulate homogeneity as an open problem.
fate: \citet[\S2, especially equation (2.3)]{griffiths1970periods} already uses the homogeneous presentation. Its underlying exposition circulated in the 1968 invited lecture and was published in 1970.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established homogeneity with the component convention stated explicitly.

title: One-dimensional formal laws and the formal inverse
notes: Over a commutative ring \(A\) with \(1\), the notes write \(F(x,y)=x+y+\sum_{i+k\ge2}a_{ik}x^iy^k\), require associativity, and obtain an inverse from the formal implicit-function argument.
statement: An associative one-dimensional formal law over \(A\) is a series \(F\in A[[x,y]]\) with \(F(x,0)=x\), \(F(0,y)=y\), and \(F(F(x,y),z)=F(x,F(y,z))\). There is a unique \(\iota(x)\in xA[[x]]\) satisfying \(F(x,\iota(x))=F(\iota(x),x)=0\); recursively \(\iota(x)=-x+O(x^2)\). Commutativity is an additional issue, recorded separately.
reconstruction: The unit identities are made explicit; they also follow from associativity and the displayed linear term. The term ``implicit-function theorem'' is formal coefficient recursion, requiring no analytic convergence.
fate: Classical definition and inverse construction: \citet[\S I]{lazard1955formal}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: an established algebraic definition.

title: Associativity does not force commutativity over every ring
notes: The parenthesis reads \ru{коммутативность (она сл. из ассоц.)}: commutativity follows from associativity.
statement: The unrestricted assertion is false. It is true over a reduced coefficient ring, and also over a torsion-free coefficient ring. Over \(\mathbb F_p[a]/(a^2)\), \(F(x,y)=x+y+axy^p\) is associative and not commutative; the notebook itself supplies this counterexample in 1972-285.6.
reconstruction: The extra hypotheses are editorial repairs, not present in this parenthesis. The counterexample is a later occurrence in the same notebook, not a conjectural interpretation. The earlier 1971-270.7 had already distinguished the characteristic-zero commutativity statement.
fate: Already distinguished in \citet[Theorem I; \S III, Remark (3.14a)]{lazard1955formal}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: the literal assertion is refuted; the corrected versions are established.

title: Strict coordinate changes versus classification of laws
notes: The change \(z=\varphi(x)=x+a_1x^2+\cdots\) defines isomorphism. The speaker expressly says that classifying laws is different from classifying their isomorphism classes.
statement: A strict isomorphism \(F\to G\) is \(\varphi\in xA[[x]]\) with \(\varphi'(0)=1\) and \(\varphi(F(x,y))=G(\varphi(x),\varphi(y))\). A general isomorphism instead allows \(\varphi'(0)\in A^\times\). The functor of laws and its quotient by coordinate changes are different classification problems.
reconstruction: The adjective ``strict'' is supplied. The inverse expansion should be \(\varphi^{-1}(z)=z-a_1z^2+\cdots\); the notebook mixes the argument \(x\) with the output variable \(z\).
fate: Classical coordinate-change action: \citet[\S I, (1.4)--(1.8)]{lazard1955formal}; earlier occurrence 1971-270.5 distinguishes full and strict changes.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: standard, with the law/moduli distinction preserved.

title: Logarithm of a formal law
notes: A series \(g(x)=x+\cdots\) is called a logarithm when \(F(x,y)=g^{-1}(g(x)+g(y))\).
statement: A normalized logarithm is a strict homomorphism \(g:F\to\widehat{\mathbb G}_a\): \(g(F(x,y))=g(x)+g(y)\), \(g(0)=0\), \(g'(0)=1\). Its formal inverse exists because its linear coefficient is a unit.
fate: Pre-lecture formulation: \citet[\S1]{honda1968formal}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: standard; integral or positive-characteristic existence is not automatic.

title: Canonical invariant differential
notes: For the shift \(x\mapsto F(x,t)\), invariance is \(\psi(F(x,t))\partial_xF(x,t)=\psi(x)\). The canonical differential is \(\omega_F=dx/\partial_yF(x,0)\).
statement: For a commutative one-dimensional formal law over a commutative ring \(A\), put \(b(x)=\partial_yF(x,y)|_{y=0}\), so \(b(0)=1\). Then \(\omega_F=b(x)^{-1}dx\) is translation invariant. Every invariant differential is \(c\omega_F\), \(c\in A\); thus normalization at the identity gives uniqueness.
reconstruction: The inverse is the formal inverse of the unit series \(b\); the parameter is held fixed during differentiation. No analytic differential form or integration is assumed.
fate: Pre-lecture invariant-differential construction: \citet[\S1]{honda1968formal}; earlier occurrences 1971-268.12 and 1971-270.8 cover invariant differentials and the logarithm.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established over arbitrary coefficient rings for commutative laws.

title: Existence and uniqueness of the normalized rational logarithm
notes: The ``Lazard lemma'' says that if \(A\) is a \(\mathbb Q\)-module, every formal group has a logarithm. The proof integrates \(\omega_F\), then evaluates at \(x=0\) to identify the integration constant.
statement: If \(A\) is a commutative unital \(\mathbb Q\)-algebra, then \(g(x)=\int_0^x b(t)^{-1}\,dt\) is the unique normalized logarithm of a commutative one-dimensional formal law. Hence any two such laws over \(A\) are uniquely strictly isomorphic by the composite of their logarithms and inverse logarithms.
reconstruction: ``\(\mathbb Q\)-module'' is interpreted as a compatible \(\mathbb Q\)-algebra structure on the given ring. The printed pointer ``Mat. 13:6'' resolves to Honda, not to a Russian publication of Lazard.
fate: \citet[\S1]{honda1968formal}: original 1968, Russian translation 1969.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: proved; denominators explain the restriction on the base.

title: The universal rational law
notes: With \(g(x)=x+\sum_{i\ge1}g_ix^{i+1}\), the ring \(\mathbb Q[g_1,g_2,\ldots]\) carries a universal law, and every law is obtained by a coefficient homomorphism.
statement: The functor sending a commutative \(\mathbb Q\)-algebra \(A\) to its commutative one-dimensional formal laws is represented by \(\mathbb Q[g_1,g_2,\ldots]\), using \(F=g^{-1}(g(x)+g(y))\). The specialization sends \(g_i\) to the normalized logarithm coefficients. This represents laws in a chosen coordinate, not isomorphism classes.
fate: Pre-lecture rational universal construction: \citet[\S1]{buchstabermishchenkonovikov1971formal}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established and consistent with rationalization of the Lazard ring.

title: Presentation of the integral universal coefficient ring
notes: The notes form \(\Lambda=\mathbb Z[a_{ij}]/J\), where \(J\) is generated by associativity coefficients and \(a_{ij}-a_{ji}\), with \(\deg a_{ij}=i+j-1\).
statement: Let \(i,j\ge1\), put \(F=x+y+\sum a_{ij}x^iy^j\), and quotient the polynomial ring by all coefficients of its associator and by all symmetry relations. For every commutative unital \(A\), ring maps \(\Lambda\to A\) correspond bijectively to commutative one-dimensional formal laws over \(A\).
reconstruction: The positive indices exclude pure higher powers and incorporate the identity laws. The grading uses half the usual topological degree.
fate: Universal property: \citet[Theorem~1.2]{buchstabermishchenkonovikov1971formal}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established; representability does not itself prove polynomiality.

title: Lazard polynomiality and rationalization
notes: \(\Lambda=\mathbb Z[a_i]\), one generator of every degree \(i\ge1\), and \(\Lambda\otimes\mathbb Q=\mathbb Q[g_i]\).
statement: The coefficient ring of the universal commutative one-dimensional formal law is noncanonically a graded polynomial ring \(\mathbb Z[t_1,t_2,\ldots]\), \(\deg t_i=i\). Under rationalization logarithm coefficients give polynomial coordinates. A choice of integral generators is not canonical.
fate: \citet[Theorem II]{lazard1955formal}; circulated December 1954, published 1955.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established; previous occurrence 1971-268.11 concerns the same universal-ring theorem.

title: Indecomposables linearize associativity
notes: The quotient by decomposables makes products of positive-degree coefficients zero and turns the associator into a linear equation for \(h=F-x-y\). A marginal gloss wrongly describes decomposables using arbitrary nonunits.
statement: For the augmented graded ring \(\Lambda\), use \(I=\bigoplus_{n>0}\Lambda_n\). Indecomposables are \(I/I^2\), or the augmented ring \(\Lambda/I^2\) if degree zero is retained. Modulo \(I^2\), associativity is \(h(x,y)+h(x+y,z)=h(y,z)+h(x,y+z)\). Products of positive-degree elements, not products of arbitrary nonunits, generate \(I^2\).
reconstruction: The margin is repaired using the unambiguous main-text phrase ``products of two of nonzero degree''. Taking nonunits literally would include integers such as \(2\) and alter degree zero.
fate: Classical linearization: \citet[\S~II, Lemma~2]{lazard1955formal}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: valid after the augmentation-ideal correction.

title: Classify homogeneous additive two-cocycles
notes: \ru{Задача: найти все решения} of \(h(x,y)+h(x+y,z)=h(y,z)+h(x,y+z)\), homogeneous polynomials over a ring \(K\). The surrounding formal-group problem requires symmetry; the page also temporarily studies nonsymmetric cycles.
statement: For each \(n\ge2\), classify normalized homogeneous \(h\in K[x,y]\) of degree \(n\) satisfying the displayed cocycle equation, and distinguish the symmetric submodule. In the symmetric case every solution is uniquely \(aC_n\), where \(C_n=((x+y)^n-x^n-y^n)/d_n\), \(d_n=p\) if \(n\) is a power of a prime \(p\), and \(d_n=1\) otherwise. This formula holds over every commutative ring via integral coefficients.
reconstruction: The exact symmetric answer is supplied from literature; the notebook states the task and develops its cohomological calculation over subsequent meetings. Nonsymmetric cycles must not be discarded before the distinction is made.
fate: Symmetric classification: \citet[\S~II, Lemma~3]{lazard1955formal}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: the symmetric problem was already solved; the lecture is an exposition, not an orphan open question.

title: Primitive polynomial Hopf algebra and comodules
notes: \(K[x]\) has \(\Delta x=x\otimes1+1\otimes x\); a comodule is described as \(N\to A\otimes N\), and \(K\) is the trivial comodule.
statement: For the graded coalgebra \(C=K[x]\) with primitive generator, a left comodule is a \(K\)-module \(N\) with coaction \(\rho:N\to C\otimes_KN\) satisfying coassociativity and the counit identity. The trivial coaction on \(K\) is \(1\mapsto1\otimes1\). Internal polynomial degree and cohomological degree produce the two gradings.
reconstruction: The base-module structure and both coaction axioms are made explicit. ``Abelian group'' alone is insufficient for a general coefficient ring.
fate: Pre-existing homological apparatus; compare \citet[Chs.VIII,X]{cartaneilenberg1956homological}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: standard with the specified category.

title: The two-cocycle exact sequence requires coalgebra cohomology
notes: The page writes \(0\to\{c((x+y)^n-x^n-y^n)\}\to L\to\operatorname{Ext}^{2,n}_{K[x]}(K,K)\to0\).
statement: For the normalized cobar complex of the primitive coalgebra \(K[x]\), \(Z^{2,n}=\{h:\delta h=0\}\), \(B^{2,n}=\{c((x+y)^n-x^n-y^n):c\in K\}\), and \(0\to B^{2,n}\to Z^{2,n}\to H^{2,n}\to0\). This is comodule cohomology (or dual divided-power algebra cohomology under suitable graded duality), not ordinary module Ext over the polynomial algebra.
reconstruction: The category is an essential emendation. Over a field, ordinary \(\operatorname{Ext}_{K[x]}^2(K,K)=0\), while the cobar group in characteristic \(p\) need not vanish. The leftmost term is the image subgroup, not an injective copy of every scalar \(c\).
fate: Cocycle/boundary calculation matches \citet[\S~II--III]{lazard1955formal}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: correct as a cobar exact sequence; the unqualified Ext notation is misleading.

title: Quadratic and cubic cocycles: a mistaken characteristic
notes: For degree 2 the notes give \(cxy\). For degree 3 they give \(C_1x^2y+C_2xy^2\), write \(\widetilde\Lambda=\mathbb Z+\mathbb Z_3\), and claim \(x^2y\) is a cocycle over \(\mathbb Z_3\)-modules.
statement: Degree2 normalized cocycles are \(cxy\). In degree 3, direct expansion gives \(\delta(C_1x^2y+C_2xy^2)=2(C_1-C_2)xyz\), with \(\delta h=h(x,y)+h(x+y,z)-h(y,z)-h(x,y+z)\). Thus \(x^2y\) is a cocycle when \(2=0\), not when \(3=0\). The universal coefficient module without symmetry is \(\mathbb Z^2/\langle2(e_1-e_2)\rangle\simeq\mathbb Z\oplus\mathbb Z/2\); imposing symmetry leaves \(\mathbb Z\).
reconstruction: \oursComputed\ The polynomial expansion and independent evaluations in characteristics 2 and 3 were both checked in the included formal-check script. The two visible subscripts3 in the scan are faithful notebook errors, not transcription corrections.
fate: Corrected symmetric case agrees with \citet[\S~II, Lemma~3]{lazard1955formal}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: the literal characteristic 3 claim is disproved by the displayed defect.

title: Minimal resolutions simplify the cohomology differential
notes: ``Choose the resolution correctly: all cycles without boundaries (minimal resolution).''
statement: For a connected graded algebra \(A\) over a field \(k\), a minimal graded free resolution of the augmentation module has differential with entries in \(A_{>0}\). Applying \(\operatorname{Hom}_A(-,k)\) makes that differential zero. Such a minimality argument does not hold unchanged over every coefficient ring.
reconstruction: The field and connected-grading hypotheses specify a valid version of the terse method; the notes have not established minimality over arbitrary \(K\).
fate: Established resolution method; \citet[Chs.III,XII]{maclane1963homology}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: standard under the stated hypotheses.

title: Divided-power multiplication on the dual
notes: \(K_*[x]=\operatorname{Hom}_K(K[x],K)\), \((x_*^n,x^m)=\delta_{nm}\), and \(x_*^nx_*^m=\binom{n+m}{n}x_*^{n+m}\).
statement: The graded dual of the primitive polynomial coalgebra has basis \(X_n\) and multiplication \(X_nX_m=\binom{n+m}{n}X_{n+m}\). This is the divided-power algebra. The full dual is its degree completion; the distinction matters when forming tensor products and duals.
reconstruction: The completion convention is supplied because the notebook initially uses full Hom, later continuous duality (P476).
fate: Standard Hopf-dual construction; \citet[Ch.X]{cartaneilenberg1956homological}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established; the displayed multiplication is independently determined by the binomial coproduct.

title: Characteristic-p factorization of the divided-power algebra
notes: The dual is written as \(\prod B_q\), with \(B_q=\mathbb Z_p[y_{p^i}]/(y_{p^i}^{p})\), and the text says it is enough to consider \(\mathbb Z_p\) and \(\mathbb Q\).
statement: Over \(k=\mathbb F_p\), the graded divided-power algebra is \(\bigotimes_{i\ge0}k[Y_i]/(Y_i^p)\), \(\deg Y_i=p^i\); its full dual version is the degree-completed tensor product. Over \(\mathbb Q\) it is isomorphic to a polynomial algebra by \(X_n\mapsto t^n/n!\). Passage from field calculations to an integral conclusion requires the finite-generation and torsion argument in each degree.
reconstruction: \(\mathbb Z_p\) here denotes the field with \(p\) elements, not the p-adic integers. An ordinary direct product of algebras would introduce unrelated idempotents and is not the asserted factorization.
fate: Established homological calculation; compare \citet[Ch.X]{cartaneilenberg1956homological}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: valid after distinguishing tensor product, completion, and coefficient fields.

title: Representations of a directed graph without imposed relations
notes: The graph is called a category; vector spaces stand at vertices and maps on arrows, with \ru{функторность не требуется}. The task is classification.
statement: For a finite quiver \(Q\) and field \(k\), a finite-dimensional representation assigns \(V_i\) to every vertex and \(A_a:V_{s(a)}\to V_{t(a)}\) to every arrow. Isomorphisms are invertible vertex maps intertwining all arrows. This is a functor from the free path category of \(Q\); no relations equating distinct paths are imposed.
reconstruction: The free path category repairs the apparent conflict between calling the graph a category and rejecting functoriality. A graph itself has no specified composites.
fate: This formulation is explicit in \citet[Definition 1, p.~17]{bernsteingelfandponomarev1973coxeter}, received 18 December 1972, and is already attributed there to Gabriel.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established with the hypotheses and distinctions stated here.

title: A single arrow requires rank as well as kernel and cokernel
notes: The only invariants of a map are said to be \(\dim\ker\) and \(\dim\operatorname{coker}\); the problem is reduced to an embedding.
statement: An arbitrary linear map between unspecified finite-dimensional spaces is classified by the triple \((\dim\ker A,\operatorname{rank}A,\dim\operatorname{coker}A)\). If source and target dimensions are fixed, rank alone is sufficient. The representation decomposes into copies of \(k\to0\), \(k\xrightarrow{1}k\), and \(0\to k\).
reconstruction: An elementary check \ours: the missing rank is essential, since the identity maps on \(k\) and \(k^2\) have equal zero kernels and cokernels but are nonisomorphic as arrow representations.
fate: The elementary matrix normal form is reviewed in \citet[Example 1, p.~750]{nazarova1973quivers}; it was classical before the talk.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established with the hypotheses and distinctions stated here.

title: One loop is the similarity problem for one operator
notes: A one-loop graph is labelled one transformation.
statement: A representation of the one-loop quiver is a finite-dimensional \(k[t]\)-module. Over an algebraically closed field it is a direct sum of Jordan blocks \(J_m(\lambda)\), uniquely up to order; over an arbitrary field use elementary divisors for monic irreducibles.
reconstruction: The notebook gives the problem, not the Jordan normal-form theorem; the latter is the precise modern resolution.
fate: The standard similarity interpretation is stated in \citet[Example 2, p.~750]{nazarova1973quivers}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established with the hypotheses and distinctions stated here.

title: Arbitrary matrix pairs reduce to commuting pairs
notes: Two loops are called an unsolvable problem; the notes say that the arbitrary pair reduces to commuting operators, citing Gelfand and Ponomarev.
statement: For finite-dimensional vector spaces over a field, simultaneous similarity of arbitrary tuples of endomorphisms embeds into classification of commuting pairs on a larger finite-dimensional space. Thus the commuting-pair problem contains the free-algebra representation problem. This is a statement about complexity of uniform classification, not algorithmic undecidability of the isomorphism test for two given pairs.
reconstruction: The word unsolvable is interpreted in its matrix-problem sense. The notebook supplies no formal undecidability claim.
fate: \citet[pp.~81--82]{gelfandponomarev1969commuting} give the construction; the note was received 23 June 1969 and published in 1969.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established with the hypotheses and distinctions stated here.

title: Classification of one or two subspaces
notes: A space with one subspace, and a space with two subspaces, are marked trivial.
statement: For ordered subspaces \(U,W\subset V\) of a finite-dimensional space, the four multiplicities \(\dim(U\cap W)\), \(\dim U-\dim(U\cap W)\), \(\dim W-\dim(U\cap W)\), and \(\dim V-\dim(U+W)\) classify the system under ambient isomorphism. The one-subspace case needs \(\dim U\) and \(\dim V/U\).
reconstruction: The explicit four complementary summands make the shorthand precise.
fate: Already the opening of \citet[section 1, p.~762]{gelfandponomarev1971quadruples} treats the two-subspace case as elementary.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established with the hypotheses and distinctions stated here.

title: Nine multiplicities classify an ordered triple of subspaces
notes: Three subspaces can be classified; \ru{Инвариантов 9, а не 8!}
statement: For finite-dimensional \((V;U_1,U_2,U_3)\), there are nine indecomposable subspace systems: eight one-dimensional systems indexed by which \(U_i\) equal the ambient line, and one two-dimensional system consisting of three distinct lines. Every system is a direct sum of these, uniquely up to ordering; the nine multiplicities are complete invariants. This is the injective-arrow subcategory of the inward \(D_4\) quiver, not all twelve indecomposable \(D_4\) representations.
reconstruction: The nine indecomposable types and the distinction from all twelve positive roots are reconstruction. The extra type is \(k^2;k e_1,k e_2,k(e_1+e_2)\).
fate: The triple case predates the talk; see \citet[section 1]{gelfandponomarev1971quadruples}. Its quiver interpretation follows the root classification in \citet[Theorem 3.1]{bernsteingelfandponomarev1973coxeter}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established with the hypotheses and distinctions stated here.

title: Four-subspace classification and continuous families
notes: Four subspaces are said to have been classified by Gelfand and Ponomarev, with infinitely many indecomposables.
statement: Ordered quadruples of subspaces in a finite-dimensional vector space over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero admit the Gelfand--Ponomarev indecomposable classification. Infinite families occur already in \(k^2\): four ordered lines \(k e_1,k e_2,k(e_1+e_2),k(e_1+\lambda e_2)\) with \(\lambda\ne0,1\) are pairwise nonisomorphic for distinct \(\lambda\).
reconstruction: The field hypothesis is the one read in the original paper. The displayed family is an illustrative check \ours: an ambient automorphism preserving the first three ordered lines is scalar, and therefore it cannot change the fourth line’s parameter.
fate: \citet[Theorem 1 and section 2]{gelfandponomarev1971quadruples}, received 21 October 1970, published 1971, is an exact prior publication.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established with the hypotheses and distinctions stated here.

title: Which quivers have only finitely many indecomposables?
notes: The question is attributed to Gabriel; the answer is Dynkin diagrams, except those with multiple arrows.
statement: For a finite connected quiver over an algebraically closed field, the set of isomorphism classes of finite-dimensional indecomposable representations is finite exactly when the underlying unoriented graph is one of \(A_n,D_n,E_6,E_7,E_8\). Every orientation works. Non-simply-laced Dynkin diagrams are not exceptions to this theorem: they are outside this ordinary-quiver list.
reconstruction: Finite-dimensionality, the coefficient field and the distinction between an ordinary quiver and a valued diagram are supplied.
fate: Gabriel’s theorem was published in 1972; its proof and exact statement are reproduced in \citet[Theorem 3.1]{bernsteingelfandponomarev1973coxeter}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established with the hypotheses and distinctions stated here.

title: The affine classification attributed to Roiter or Nazarova
notes: The theorem is assigned to an uncertain \ru{Ройтов} from Kyiv or \ru{Назаровы}: a class of diagrams admits classification like that of four subspaces.
statement: The identifiable content is the finite/tame boundary for ordinary quivers: connected quivers of infinite tame type have underlying extended Dynkin graphs (including the loop and Kronecker limiting cases under the usual conventions); all other infinite types contain the simultaneous-matrix-pair problem.
reconstruction: Roiter and Nazarova are bibliographically plausible normalized names; the scan does not establish a separate Roiter theorem or joint authorship.
fate: \citet[section 1, theorem, pp.~752--753]{nazarova1973quivers} is the exact match. It was received 19 September 1972 and published in 1973, so the notebook reports an already circulating result.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established with the hypotheses and distinctions stated here.

title: Dynkin diagrams also arise in hypersurface singularities
notes: Gelfand points to a connection with singularities and names Artin, Tyurina and Brieskorn.
statement: The bounded identification supported here is the common simply-laced ADE diagrams: they classify simple complex hypersurface singularities (up to stabilization/right equivalence) and finite-type quivers. The notebook states no functor between these categories and no equivalence of their deformation theories.
reconstruction: Only the common classification diagrams are identified; a categorical correspondence would go beyond the notes.
fate: The singularity classification is in \citet[sections 1--2 and 9]{arnold1972normal}, received 21 June 1972. Records 284 and 294 expand this connection.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established with the hypotheses and distinctions stated here.

title: The category of representations and direct sums
notes: \(\operatorname{Cat}(\Gamma)\) has vector spaces over vertices, maps over arrows and commuting vertexwise morphisms. Direct sum is defined, and the note stresses that isomorphic objects need not be identified.
statement: For a fixed finite quiver \(Q\), \(\operatorname{Rep}_k(Q)\) is the category described in 1972-277.1, retaining actual objects and all intertwining morphisms. Direct sums are taken at each vertex and on each arrow. Passing to a set of isomorphism classes loses the category structure needed for functors.
fate: See \citet[Definition 1 and p.~18]{bernsteingelfandponomarev1973coxeter}. This is the already established categorical formulation, not a new theorem of October 1972.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established with the hypotheses and distinctions stated here.

title: Krull--Schmidt decomposition
notes: Every object is a sum of indecomposables, uniquely up to isomorphism.
statement: Every finite-dimensional quiver representation is a finite direct sum of nonzero indecomposables. The multiset of their isomorphism classes and multiplicities is unique. The zero object corresponds to the empty sum. Finite total vector-space dimension gives existence and the finite-dimensional endomorphism rings give the Krull--Schmidt property.
reconstruction: Finite-dimensionality and uniqueness up to permutation are made explicit.
fate: Explicitly recalled in \citet[p.~18 and footnote 2]{bernsteingelfandponomarev1973coxeter}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established with the hypotheses and distinctions stated here.

title: Gabriel classification for every orientation
notes: The connected graphs \(A_n,D_n,E_6,E_7,E_8\) are drawn; arrows may be placed arbitrarily.
statement: The finite-type statement is exactly 1972-277.8. It concerns finitely many indecomposables across all dimension vectors, not finitely many orbits merely in a fixed representation space.
fate: \citet[Theorem 3.1]{bernsteingelfandponomarev1973coxeter} reprove Gabriel’s 1972 result; the BGP manuscript was received 18 December 1972.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established with the hypotheses and distinctions stated here.

title: Obstructions to finite type from cycles and branching
notes: The notes exclude cycles because eigenvalues appear, a four-armed star, and a chain with forks at both ends.
statement: A cycle supports infinitely many nonisomorphic representations by varying the monodromy around its underlying unoriented cycle, taking inverse arrow maps where needed and choosing all these maps invertible. The four-subspace star is \(\widetilde D_4\), and the two-fork diagrams are extended \(D\)-type; each has infinite representation type. Extending these representations by zero or along identity edges gives obstructions inside larger graphs. This is only part of the necessity proof.
reconstruction: The notebook sketches excluded shapes; the extension operations and the warning that the list is only partial are editorial.
fate: The full necessity argument is Tits’s quadratic-form proof in \citet[proof of Theorem 3.1, pp.~28--29]{bernsteingelfandponomarev1973coxeter}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established with the hypotheses and distinctions stated here.

title: Positive roots are the indecomposable dimension vectors
notes: The number of indecomposables is independent of arrow directions. With \(\gamma=\sum n_i\alpha_i\), the coefficients \(n_i\) are dimensions and each root gives an indecomposable.
statement: For a Dynkin quiver, dimension vector induces a bijection between indecomposable isomorphism classes and positive roots of the associated simply-laced root system. Thus an indecomposable is uniquely determined by its dimension vector, and the number is \(|\Phi^+|\), independent of orientation.
reconstruction: The restriction to finite Dynkin type is essential: dimension vectors do not classify arbitrary quiver representations.
fate: \citet[Theorem 3.1(2)]{bernsteingelfandponomarev1973coxeter}, citing Gabriel 1972, states this precise bijection.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established with the hypotheses and distinctions stated here.

title: The notebook counts simple roots instead of positive roots
notes: After defining positive roots, the next line says \ru{кол-во = кол-ву простых корней}.
statement: The correct count is the number of positive roots: \(n(n+1)/2\) for \(A_n\), \(n(n-1)\) for \(D_n\), and \(36,63,120\) for \(E_6,E_7,E_8\). The number of simple roots is only the number of vertices.
reconstruction: This is an emendation of a faithfully transcribed notebook error, not a translation error.
fate: The correction follows from \citet[Theorem 3.1(2)]{bernsteingelfandponomarev1973coxeter}; the six rows immediately below the handwritten sentence already contradict its literal reading for \(A_3\).
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established with the hypotheses and distinctions stated here.

title: The six interval representations of A3
statement: For \(1\to2\to3\), the six indecomposables are the interval representations \([i,j]\), \(1\le i\le j\le3\): one-dimensional spaces at vertices in the interval, zero elsewhere, and identity internal arrows.
fate: This is the \(A_3\) instance of \citet[Theorem 3.1]{bernsteingelfandponomarev1973coxeter}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established with the hypotheses and distinctions stated here.

title: What the notebook calls an unsolvable category
notes: The category of two arbitrary operators is denoted \(C\). An embedding \(C\to\operatorname{Cat}(\Gamma)\) taking nonisomorphic objects to nonisomorphic ones is used to define unsolvable.
statement: The intended modern notion is wildness: a representation embedding from finite-dimensional \(k\langle x,y\rangle\)-modules into the category, given by an exact k-linear functor with the standard bimodule or algebraic control, preserving indecomposability and reflecting isomorphism. A bare injection on isomorphism classes does not characterize wildness and is too weak to distinguish tame families.
reconstruction: The exact representation-embedding requirements are modern repairs. No decision-theoretic impossibility is inferred from the notebook word.
fate: The matrix-pair containment criterion is the one used in \citet[Introduction and section 1]{nazarova1973quivers}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established with the hypotheses and distinctions stated here.

title: Extended Dynkin quivers have tame infinite type
notes: The solvable graphs are said to be extended Dynkin diagrams, with cycle and affine \(D,E\) sketches; their relation with reflection groups is mentioned.
statement: For finite connected ordinary quivers over an algebraically closed field, tame infinite type corresponds to the extended simply-laced Dynkin graphs, with the standard loop/cycle and Kronecker conventions. Finite Dynkin graphs remain finite type, hence are also classifiable. For fixed dimension, tame type means finitely many one-parameter families apart from finitely many exceptions.
reconstruction: The finite-type graphs must be added if solvable includes finite classification. The notebook does not define one-parameter families or deal separately with limiting affine conventions.
fate: Exact matching classification: \citet[section 1, theorem]{nazarova1973quivers}, submitted 19 September 1972 and published 1973 (English translation 1974).
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established with the hypotheses and distinctions stated here.

title: Lazard theorem restated through indecomposables
notes: \(\Lambda=\mathbb Z[a_1,a_2,\ldots]\), \(\deg a_n=n\ge1\); the proposed proof passes to \(\bar\Lambda=\Lambda/(\text{decomposables})\).
statement: The universal commutative formal-law ring is polynomial; its positive indecomposables form one free rank-one group in every positive degree. Linearized relations describe those indecomposables, but a generation and torsion argument is still needed to recover the polynomial ring.
reconstruction: The phrase ``universal ring for polynomials'' is read degree by degree as a representing coefficient module with square-zero multiplication in positive degree.
fate: Restatement of \citet[Theorem II]{lazard1955formal}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established; no separate publication or new result is implied by this repeat.

title: An equivalent symmetric cocycle identity
statement: For a symmetric normalized polynomial \(h\), the identity displayed in the notes is equivalent to \(h(x,y)+h(x+y,z)=h(y,z)+h(x,y+z)\). To recover the latter, interchange \(x\) and \(z\) in the former and use symmetry.
reconstruction: The equation is not a mistranscription of the usual cocycle identity; it is equivalent in the explicitly stated symmetric context.
fate: Same cocycle class as \citet[\S~II, Lemma~3]{lazard1955formal}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: correct with the symmetry hypothesis retained.

title: Resolution of the primitive coalgebra
notes: The sequence \(A[x]\to A[x]\otimes\bar A[y]\to A[x]\otimes\bar A[y]\otimes\bar A[z]\to\cdots\) is called a bar resolution; \(\bar A[y]\) has zero constant term.
statement: For the coaugmented coalgebra \(C=A[x]\), use the normalized cofree comodule resolution, whose reduced factors are \(\bar C=\ker\varepsilon\). The associated cobar cochain groups are \(A\), \(\bar C\), \(\bar C^{\otimes2}\), and so on; the differential inserts the reduced coproduct with alternating signs.
reconstruction: ``Cobar'' and ``comodule'' specify the variance omitted by the notebook. The polynomial coalgebra is free as an \(A\)-module, so the relative normalized construction has the needed underlying-module exactness.
fate: Classical bar/cobar apparatus; \citet[Ch.X]{cartaneilenberg1956homological}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: standard once the category is fixed.

title: Ordinary module Hom cannot substitute for comodule Hom
notes: The notes label the functor \(\operatorname{Hom}_{A[x]}(\mathcal A,A)\), call the resolution terms \(A[x]\)-modules, and obtain polynomial cochains.
statement: The intended polynomial cochains arise from \(\operatorname{Hom}_{C\text{-comod}}(A,-)\), or from continuous Hom over the dual divided-power algebra. They do not arise from the displayed ordinary polynomial-module Ext computation. For a field \(k\), the two-term free resolution \(0\to k[x]\xrightarrow{x}k[x]\to k\to0\) proves \(\operatorname{Ext}^2_{k[x]}(k,k)=0\).
reconstruction: \ours\ The displayed two-term free resolution independently proves the vanishing of ordinary module Ext in degree two. This is a mathematical notation repair confirmed by the explicit dual algebra introduced on P476. It does not assert that the speaker intended the incorrect ordinary-module calculation.
fate: The resolution distinction is standard; \citet[Chs.~VIII, X]{cartaneilenberg1956homological}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: the category omission must remain visible in any faithful edition.

title: Normalized coboundaries and the four-term differential
notes: The boundary of \(x^n\) is \((x+y)^n-x^n-y^n\). A later shorthand writes only two terms for the differential of \(h\), and notes that reduction removes constant terms.
statement: The normalized cobar differential is \(d f(x,y)=f(x+y)-f(x)-f(y)\), and \(d h(x,y,z)=h(x+y,z)-h(y,z)-h(x,y+z)+h(x,y)\). Thus degree-two cycles are precisely additive cocycles. The two displayed substitution terms require their reduced-coproduct corrections.
reconstruction: The four-term formula is supplied explicitly to disambiguate the abbreviated P467 formula; P476 later records all four terms correctly.
fate: Classical cocycle differential: \citet[\S~II, Lemma~2]{lazard1955formal}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established; the normalized and unreduced versions should not be mixed.

title: Formal unitization of an associative ring
notes: For an associative ring \(A\), not necessarily with identity, \(iA\) formally adjoins an identity, with \(A\) a two-sided ideal and \(iA/A=\mathbb Z\); \(i\) is a functor.
statement: For any associative ring \(A\), define \(iA=\mathbb Z\oplus A\) additively, with \((m,a)(n,b)=(mn,mb+na+ab)\). Its identity is \((1,0)\), the map \(A\to iA\), \(a\mapsto(0,a)\), identifies an ideal, and \(iA/A\cong\mathbb Z\). Every ring homomorphism induces the identity on \(\mathbb Z\) and the given map on \(A\).
reconstruction: The multiplication, implicit in formal adjoining, is written explicitly. Even if \(A\) already has an identity, this formal unitization is not being identified with \(A\) itself.
fate: The exact framework appears in \citet{vaserstein1973foundations}, received on 14 November 1972, the day after this talk; the detailed treatment \citet{vaserstein1976foundations} was received on 26 February 1975 and published in 1976. See \citet[\S1, pp.~100--101]{vaserstein1976foundations}. The elementary unitization construction itself is antecedent background, so its occurrence is E.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: standard functorial unitization used to organize nonunital K theory.

title: Quasiunits under the circle product
notes: The law \(a\circ b=a+b+ab\) is associative, and \(GA\subset A\) is its group of invertible elements with identity zero. The map \(a\mapsto1+a\) is described as a homomorphism into ordinary units.
statement: The operation \(\circ\) makes \(A\) a monoid with identity zero. Its invertible elements are precisely \(GA=\{a\in A:1+a\in(iA)^\times\}\), and \(a\mapsto1+a\) identifies this group with the units of \(iA\) congruent to one modulo \(A\). Ring homomorphisms preserve quasiunits and give a group-valued functor \(G\).
reconstruction: The map from all of \(A\) lands in the multiplicative monoid \(1+A\), not necessarily its unit group; only its restriction to \(GA\) lands in units. For example, \(-1\) in a nonzero unital ring is not quasiinvertible.
fate: The exact framework appears in \citet{vaserstein1973foundations}, received on 14 November 1972, the day after this talk; the detailed treatment \citet{vaserstein1976foundations} was received on 26 February 1975 and published in 1976. The precise quasiunit convention is \citet[\S2, p.~101]{vaserstein1976foundations}.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: the quasiunit construction is standard; the literal unrestricted units statement needs correction.

title: Finite matrix stabilization and the stable general linear group
notes: The notes introduce \(M_kA\), the finite-support matrix ring \(MA\), and its quasiunit group \(GMA\).
statement: Let \(M_kA\) be the ring of \(k\times k\) matrices and \(MA=\bigcup_k M_kA\) under upper-left embeddings with zero complementary block. For unital \(A\), the map \(a\mapsto I+a\) identifies \(GMA\) with the stable group \(\mathrm{GL}(A)=\varinjlim_k\mathrm{GL}_k(A)\), whose stabilization adjoins identity blocks.
reconstruction: The zero-block and identity-block stabilization conventions agree only after the change from circle coordinates to ordinary multiplicative coordinates. The finite-support ring \(MA\) is not itself unital when \(A\ne0\).
fate: The exact framework appears in \citet{vaserstein1973foundations}, received on 14 November 1972, the day after this talk; the detailed treatment \citet{vaserstein1976foundations} was received on 26 February 1975 and published in 1976. See \citet[\S3, p.~101]{vaserstein1976foundations}. These standard matrix conventions are also the background of 1971-256.1.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: standard stable matrix group, with both coordinate conventions distinguished.

title: Row-and-column-finite cone and suspension rings
notes: The ring \(\widetilde\Omega A\) consists of infinite matrices with finitely many nonzero entries in every row and column; \(MA\) is its finite-support two-sided ideal, and \(\Omega A=\widetilde\Omega A/MA\).
statement: With indices in \(\mathbb N\), row-and-column-finite matrices over any associative ring form a ring under ordinary matrix multiplication: each entry is a finite sum and row and column finiteness are preserved. Finite-support matrices form a two-sided ideal. The quotient is the notebook's suspension ring. All three constructions are functorial in \(A\).
reconstruction: The tilde distinguishes the cone from its quotient throughout this chapter; later sources use different Omega decorations. No boundedness condition on the number of entries per row is imposed by these notes.
fate: The exact framework appears in \citet{vaserstein1973foundations}, received on 14 November 1972, the day after this talk; the detailed treatment \citet{vaserstein1976foundations} was received on 26 February 1975 and published in 1976. The definitions occur at the start of the 1973 announcement and in \citet[\S3]{vaserstein1976foundations}. Earlier occurrences are 1971-253.5 and 1971-256.2.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: established cone/suspension machinery; the later vanishing theorem is a separate item.

title: Strict triangular matrices and their quasiinverses
notes: The subring \(\Theta A\) is called upper triangular but is defined by \(a_{ij}=0\) for \(i\leq j\); the page says \(G\Theta A=\Theta A\) because its matrices are nilpotent.
statement: Choose either strict upper triangular finite-support matrices, with \(a_{ij}=0\) for \(i\geq j\), or the transposed lower convention. Every such matrix \(a\) is nilpotent, and its circle inverse is the finite sum \(-a+a^2-a^3+\cdots\). Thus the triangular ring is a group under \(\circ\). The union over coordinate permutations is the same with either choice of orientation.
reconstruction: The word upper and the written inequality disagree in the handwriting. The choice is harmless for the subsequent permutation-triangular construction, but the two conventions are not presented as literally identical definitions.
fate: \citet[\S3 and \S11]{vaserstein1976foundations} uses triangular matrices in the same simplicial construction; the nilpotent inverse is the elementary geometric-series identity.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: standard nilpotent quasiunit subgroup with a recorded orientation inconsistency.

title: Reindexing requires injective maps
notes: A bijection \(\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) simultaneously permutes rows and columns and is called an inner automorphism. The next sentence claims that even any map \(\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) gives an endomorphism.
statement: Every injection \(e:\mathbb N\hookrightarrow\mathbb N\) gives a ring embedding \(MA\to MA\) by placing \(a_{ij}\) in position \((e(i),e(j))\) and filling other entries with zero; bijections give automorphisms. Arbitrary noninjective reindexings do not preserve matrix multiplication. For unital \(A\), a permutation is implemented by conjugation in the larger row-and-column-finite matrix ring, but need not be inner in the finitary stable group.
reconstruction: \ours\ A collapsed pair of indices sends two orthogonal diagonal matrix units \(E_{11},E_{22}\) over \(\mathbb Z\) to the same \(E_{kk}\): their original product is zero and the product of their images is not. Thus injectivity is indispensable. The ambient meaning of inner is supplied separately.
fate: \citet[\S4, pp.~101--102]{vaserstein1976foundations} correctly uses embeddings of \(\mathbb N\); it matches the repaired statement, not the arbitrary-map wording.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: the notebook's arbitrary-map assertion is false; the injection construction is elementary and established.

title: Permutation-triangular simplices and the based space S A
notes: A finite \(X\subset GMA\) is a simplex if a common left translation followed by a coordinate permutation carries it into \(\Theta A\). The distinguished vertex is zero, and the resulting simplicial scheme is \(SA\). Volodin is credited for its use in K theory.
statement: In multiplicative coordinates for unital \(A\), let \(U_\prec\) be the stable unitriangular subgroup for a total coordinate order obtained by a permutation. A finite vertex set \(X\subset\mathrm{GL}(A)\) is a simplex exactly when \(X\subset gU_\prec\) for some \(g\) and one order \(\prec\). The identity is the base vertex. This defines an abstract simplicial complex and functorial maps under ring homomorphisms.
reconstruction: A single translation and a single order must work for the whole set. Replacing this by a separate order for each pair changes the complex. The literal coordinate model is kept distinct from more general module-flag versions. The notebook's zero vertex corresponds to \(I\).
fate: \citet[\S1]{volodin1971extraordinary} had already published a flag-based simplicial approach in 1971, from a manuscript received on 27 July 1970. Its general module-flag formulation should not be confused term by term with every coordinate convention of this talk. The exact framework appears in \citet{vaserstein1973foundations}, received on 14 November 1972, the day after this talk; the detailed treatment \citet{vaserstein1976foundations} was received on 26 February 1975 and published in 1976. The left-translation definition is explicit in the 1973 announcement; \citet[\S11, Remark~(b), pp.~110--111]{vaserstein1976foundations} uses the right-translation version and identifies the two via inversion. See also 1971-253.1 and 1971-256.1.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: an identified early simplicial K-theory model; its false tolerance assertion is separately audited below.

title: Positive K groups from homotopy groups under the stated unit hypothesis
notes: The page explicitly begins \ru{Пусть в кольце A есть единица} before defining \(K_nA=\pi_{n-1}SA\), \(n\geq1\). It notes the usual group structure for \(n\geq2\) and automatic abelianity for \(n\geq3\).
statement: For an associative unital ring \(A\), define the positive groups in this model by \(K_n(A)=\pi_{n-1}(|SA|,I)\) for \(n\geq1\), with \(K_1\) initially the based set of components until its group law is supplied. This unital Volodin-type model agrees with algebraic K theory after the comparison theorem. The displayed formula alone does not define \(K_0\) or negative groups.
reconstruction: The unital hypothesis is genuinely on the scan and is not an editorial repair. The notation \(\pi\) is interpreted via realization, equivalently the combinatorial homotopy model used in the later paper. Nonunital groups require the relative/unitization construction and must not be substituted into this formula without further hypotheses.
fate: \citet[\S1]{volodin1971extraordinary} had already published a flag-based simplicial approach in 1971, from a manuscript received on 27 July 1970. Its general module-flag formulation should not be confused term by term with every coordinate convention of this talk. The exact framework appears in \citet{vaserstein1973foundations}, received on 14 November 1972, the day after this talk; the detailed treatment \citet{vaserstein1976foundations} was received on 26 February 1975 and published in 1976. \citet[Corollary~15.1 and Chapter~V]{vaserstein1976foundations} gives the unital identification and comparison. The general comparison is already tracked by GP-1971-21, but this page poses no new comparison question.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: an established model for unital positive algebraic K theory; no claim for arbitrary nonunital rings is inferred.

title: Whitehead stabilization homotopy and five block matrices
notes: Reindexing a sphere map is said not to change its homotopy class. The proof moves a finite matrix block using five circle-coordinate matrices: \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&0\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&a\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&a\\-I&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&0\\-I&a\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&0\\0&a\end{smallmatrix}\right)\).
statement: For a unital ring and a based simplicial representative of a homotopy class in \(SA\), every injective coordinate reindexing induces the same homotopy class. After reducing to a finite block and a block swap, consecutive maps in the displayed five-step construction are contiguous, giving a homotopy from a matrix block to its shifted copy. All entries \(-I\) belong to the ring because the unit hypothesis is in force.
reconstruction: Finite-block reduction is made for a finite simplicial representative; it is not an assertion that an arbitrary continuous map has a literal image consisting of finitely many vertices. This is a specific simplicial implementation of the older Whitehead stabilization idea.
fate: The exact framework appears in \citet{vaserstein1973foundations}, received on 14 November 1972, the day after this talk; the detailed treatment \citet{vaserstein1976foundations} was received on 26 February 1975 and published in 1976. The exact five-block method and its contiguity checks occur in \citet[Lemma~13.1 and Theorem~13.1, pp.~112--114]{vaserstein1976foundations}; class A concerns this implementation, not priority for Whitehead's original lemma.
present_status: As of 9 November 2026: the detailed stabilization construction is published and valid with the stated unit convention.

title: Elementary simplicial homotopy is contiguity
notes: Maps \(s_1,s_2\) are elementarily homotopic when \(s_1X\cup s_2X\) is a simplex for every source simplex \(X\). The line naming the domains and codomains reuses \(S'\) inconsistently.
statement: Two simplicial maps \(s_1,s_2:S\to T\) are contiguous if, for each simplex \(X\) of \(S\), the union \(s_1(X)\cup s_2(X)\) is a simplex of \(T\). Their realizations are homotopic; a finite chain of such contiguities gives the combinatorial homotopies used here.
